tools.model: OpenEvidence Model Family — Osler (fast, default, ~5s), Sackett (deeper search, ~30s), Snow (successor to Deep Consult, ~5 min), Darwin (frontier reasoning model, research preview, application-only)
tools.modelFamily: OpenEvidence Model Family (Osler / Sackett / Snow / Darwin) — proprietary, base architecture never disclosed
tools.notes: OpenEvidence released a named model family on 2026-09-03: Osler (fast, default, ~5s), Sackett (deeper search, ~30s), Snow (successor to Deep Consult, ~5 min), plus Darwin (frontier reasoning model, research preview and API by application only). All three production models are user-selectable via a model selector in the interface and free for verified clinicians. The stack is custom domain-specialized LLMs trained on licensed peer-reviewed literature (NEJM, JAMA specialty journals, NCCN, Springer Nature) and deliberately not on the open internet, trained and served on Baseten (Baseten Training + Baseten Embeddings Inference; end-to-end latency 700ms to 160ms; 'billions of custom, fine-tuned LLM calls per week'), with a corpus-anchored retrieval layer that selects the most relevant papers and grades evidence strength (EvidenceGrade, GRADE-inspired). Frontend is Next.js on Vercel; backend is Python/ML. No base model, parameter count, or architecture is disclosed for any of the four models; CEO Daniel Nadler describes an 'ensemble architecture' of roughly half a dozen smaller specialized models (retrieval, ranking, synthesis) rather than one large model. Separately, Reuters reported on 2026-09-22 that Anthropic's technology provides back-end support for the free, locally adapted OpenEvidence rollout across ~100 low- and middle-income countries — the only public sign that any part of OpenEvidence runs on Claude. Note on benchmark comparability: OpenEvidence reports Darwin at 82.7% on HealthBench Professional using its own setup (public test set minus multi-turn cases, Anthropic-published LLM-as-a-judge rubric grading with Claude Opus 4.8), while OpenAI reports GPT-6 Astra at 63.4% length-adjusted on the same benchmark. Different graders and task subsets mean the two numbers are not directly comparable — check each source's stated setup before drawing a conclusion.
tools.conflict: Baseten's training case study says OpenEvidence trains 'custom open-source models' but never names a base model, so 'fine-tuned open-weight base model' is inference, not disclosure. The 2026-09-03 model-family announcement is product naming, not a technical spec — it does not say whether Osler/Sackett/Snow/Darwin are single models or ensembles, nor whether Darwin uses Claude. The Anthropic partnership is a back-end technology relationship for the global/LMIC edition only; there is no evidence the US product's answers are Claude-generated. The pre-September-2026 default model was never named. A third-party systems-design essay speculates on H100 fleet sizing, LoRA/PEFT adapters and cross-encoder rerankers — plausible but unverified by the vendor, so not treated as fact.

stack.v: Licensed journals, NCCN, Cochrane — not the open internet
Ensemble of ~6 specialised models (retrieval, ranking, synthesis)

tools.notes: OpenAI's own ChatGPT for Clinicians plan page states 'Higher limits on GPT-6 — our most capable model for healthcare'. GPT-6 Astra launched Sep 3-4 2026 as the first GPT-6 model; the family expanded with Sol and Luna on Sep 22, and OpenAI's release log lists GPT-6.1 Sol (Sep 29) and GPT-6.1 Terra (Oct 26). Astra set the state of the art on HealthBench Professional, OpenAI's benchmark of real clinician tasks (care consult, documentation, medical research), scoring 63.4% length-adjusted against GPT-5.6 Sol at 60.5%. The product includes trusted clinical search with citations, deep research, CME credits, and pre-built skills. Conversation content is not used to train OpenAI's models, and the workspace is HIPAA-ready with a BAA for eligible individual accounts.
tools.conflict: OpenAI's two healthcare pages disagree. The clinician plan page says 'Higher limits on GPT-6', but the organisation-facing healthcare page still says 'Powered by our latest GPT-5 models optimized for healthcare'. Resolved to GPT-6: it is the more specific, more recently updated product page, and GPT-6 is strictly newer than any GPT-5. Note the site's own competitor tracker still lists GPT-5.4 for this product — that is stale.

tools.notes: Doximity Ask (renamed from Doximity GPT in May 2026) is described by Doximity as a composite clinical reference platform: retrieval-augmented generation over a physician-governed evidence library, multi-turn agentic tool use through a fixed registry of validated calculators, and a post-trained reasoning model that orchestrates retrieval, tool calls and citation-grounded generation. Doximity deliberately does not name the base model. What is public is the training path: Fireworks AI documents that when a frontier provider began phasing out the supervised fine-tuning Doximity was using, Doximity instead trained its own open models using its clinical expertise and physician feedback, and serves them at clinical speed. Doximity Ask went on to outperform GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Fable 5 in the independent Stanford-Harvard NOHARM safety evaluation. Citation metadata is never generated from model memory — DOI, PMID, authors and URLs are resolved through a dedicated bibliography service. Doximity offers Instant and Thinking modes, so the user does choose a reasoning tier. Renamed May 2026.
tools.conflict: Doximity's own engineering article names no model family, only 'a post-trained reasoning model'. Fireworks (Doximity's training partner) says it 'trains open models' without naming the base. Third-party trackers name specific bases for Doximity GPT/Ask that Doximity has never confirmed. Recorded as reported at family level rather than naming a base model Doximity does not confirm.

tools.notes: UpToDate Expert AI is the generative-AI layer over Wolters Kluwer's UpToDate content. Wolters Kluwer runs an explicitly 'model agnostic' Expert AI strategy and does not pin a single model: it says that by 'moving to the latest models' it significantly increased clinical relevance, and that it deploys OpenAI technologies through its secure FAB enablement platform while staying inside customer governance. An expanded enterprise AI collaboration with OpenAI was announced on June 3, 2026. The product is deliberately 'contained within the rigorously curated UpToDate content' to avoid the extraneous-data risk it attributes to open models. As of April 30, more than half of US Enterprise Edition customers representing roughly 2,000 hospitals had signed up for the Expert AI version of UpToDate Enterprise, with momentum toward 70% adoption by mid-year. The model itself is not user-selectable; what varies is the depth of search and the answer length.
tools.conflict: Wolters Kluwer never names a specific GPT version for UpToDate Expert AI — 'the latest models' is the actual published claim — so the entry records OpenAI models without pinning a version, rather than inferring one. Note the site previously recorded 'GPT-5' for this tool in benchmark contexts; those were the benchmark's comparison models, not UpToDate's production stack.

tools.modelFamily: Mixed: OpenAI GPT-5.x frontier + Abridge in-house + NVIDIA Nemotron-derived
tools.notes: Abridge explicitly runs a multi-model stack and refuses to name one model: frontier models for high-value reasoning plus purpose-built in-house models for ASR, per-section note generation and ICD-10 coding. Their most recent tech-blog post (Oct 2026) describes an LLM-based clinical ASR model (audio encoder + projector + LLM backbone, SFT then GSPO reinforcement learning) that beats Whisper-large-v3, Qwen3-ASR-1.7B, GPT-4o, GPT-Realtime-2, Gemini 3.1 Pro and Gemini 3.5 Flash on WER and medical-term miss rate; the base LLM is not named. On Jun 11 2026 Abridge and NVIDIA announced a first-of-its-kind foundation model for clinical conversations built on the NVIDIA Nemotron open model family, trained on Blackwell with pre-/mid-/post-training on de-identified data, exclusive to Abridge's platform and expected later in 2026. Model selection is explicitly not exposed to the customer — 'selecting and orchestrating the right model for each task is our responsibility' — and model changes are communicated through a partner release-update process. Clinical decision support is grounded with a curated evidence library (UpToDate, NEJM, JAMA, Wolters Kluwer, ADA, AAFP, Neurology, JCO) with citations, integrated with Epic, Oracle Health and athenahealth.
tools.conflict: Sources disagree on which frontier model is live because Abridge uses different models per task: the nursing flowsheet blog (May 2026) names GPT-5.4, the CDS/note-generation blog (Apr 2026) names GPT-5.5, and CEO Shiv Rao said in an April 2026 interview that roughly 70-80% of what Abridge does is driven by in-house models with ~30% involving a frontier model. Resolved to GPT-5.5 as the most recently named frontier model, with GPT-5.4 still named for nursing and the Nemotron model pending.

tools.model: OpenAI GPT-5 (reasoning) combined with Ambience's own proprietary AI reasoning models; ASR is in-house fine-tuned streaming speech models plus a chart-grounded reconciliation LLM
tools.notes: Ambience says its platform is 'powered by proprietary AI reasoning models', and for point-of-care CDI and Chart Chat it names OpenAI explicitly — built on 'OpenAI GPT-5's advanced reasoning capabilities with Ambience's proprietary models', with the coding model trained using OpenAI's Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (the ICD-10 model that beat board-certified physicians by a 27% relative margin). Ambience has deliberately moved up the stack from models to infrastructure: Ambience Chorus (announced Aug 2026) is the shared AI infrastructure and agent harness — a System of Context maintaining a source-linked understanding of the patient across the longitudinal chart, plus a System of Action. On the audio side (Sep 2026) Ambience runs two in-house fine-tuned streaming ASR models in parallel (a large one for narrative structure, a small one specialised for medical terminology) arbitrated by a reconciliation LLM grounded in the patient's chart, inside a rolling-window ensemble. No user-selectable model — 'Ambience Standard' prices on outcomes rather than tokens or seats. Cloud/SaaS via the Microsoft Azure Marketplace since Apr 2025, with Epic, Oracle Health/Cerner and athenahealth integrations; no vendor statement of on-premises deployment. Chart Chat is grounded in BMJ Best Practice with citations.

tools.modelFamily: Undisclosed (proprietary + commercial LLM mix; Whisper-derived ASR)
tools.notes: Nabla has deliberately stopped naming frontier models: its Sep 2026 explainer states it combines proprietary and commercial models, each selected for the performance it brings to a specific step of clinical documentation, and that Nabla trains its own smaller specialised models for precise documentation tasks in French and English rather than one big model. The help centre confirms notes are generated 'using a combination of in-house natural language algorithms and Large Language Model (LLMs)'. The only model lineage Nabla has named publicly is the speech layer: 'our model is based on Whisper', fine-tuned on 7,000 hours of manually annotated medical encounter audio, with added hallucination suppression and medical-term accuracy. Integrity is enforced by an atomic-fact verification pass — every note is split into atomic facts checked back against the transcript and patient context before the note is written. A trust-centre AI Model Card (CHAI version 3, Apr 2026) is available only on request, so the underlying models are not public. Nabla hosts on Google Cloud (US for US clients, Belgium/EU otherwise) with speech-to-text via Microsoft Azure, and holds an exclusive partnership with AMI (Yann LeCun's world-model company) for future agentic, FDA-certifiable systems. No user-selectable model; clinicians choose note templates, custom instructions and a personal medical dictionary instead.
tools.conflict: Historical sources name OpenAI models — GPT-3 at Copilot launch (Mar 2023), GPT-4 by late 2023 — and press in Jan 2024 described a migration to open-source models. These are stale; Nabla's own most recent public statement (Sep 2026) names no model at all, so the current stack is best characterised as undisclosed rather than GPT-4 or open-source.

tools.notes: Heidi's most recent and most specific model disclosure (Oct 2026) is about speech: it moved off closed vendor ASR to its own stack, fine-tuning the open NVIDIA Parakeet V2 0.6B TDT model on 1,500 hours of curated clinical audio with NVIDIA NeMo and 8x H100s, reaching 9.4% WER and a 93.5% medical-terms F1 (vs 13% WER for its legacy vendor solution), cutting latency from ~3.0s to ~0.7s and OpEx 64%, with 'full model ownership' enabling deployment in any region or private cloud. It is also testing NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Speech-to-Speech for voice agents. For the language side Heidi has not published which LLM writes notes; what is public is the routing architecture — a 'Bedrock for speed, EKS for control' hybrid (Amazon Bedrock for immediate regional compliance, self-hosted open-weight models on Amazon EKS for control), plus an earlier Google Cloud partnership providing 'clinically tuned models and speech-to-text' via Vertex AI Model Garden. The one named LLM is Claude, and only for Heidi Evidence (launched Feb 2026), 'in part built on Claude, Anthropic's AI models', grounding answers in HealthPathways, EMGuidance, MIMS, Vidal, NICE and BMJ Group content with citations. Heidi II (Sep 2026) added agents, memory and journal-grounded answers; clinician approval gates every write-back. No user-selectable model.
tools.conflict: Third-party trackers name Gemini/GPT-family models for Heidi's note generation and Anthropic Claude for Evidence, but Heidi itself only ever names Claude for Evidence, so the Scribe LLM attribution is reported rather than disclosed. The Oct 2026 Nemotron/Parakeet ASR stack supersedes the earlier Google Cloud-based speech stack.

tools.model: Fine-tuned foundation model on Azure OpenAI (base model not named by Microsoft)
tools.notes: Dragon Copilot (formerly Dragon Ambient, the DAX/DAX Copilot lineage) is Microsoft's clinical workflow AI. Microsoft describes it as bringing together voice dictation and ambient listening with 'fine-tuned generative AI and healthcare-adapted safeguards', and its transparency documentation describes the service as running on Azure OpenAI with Azure OpenAI Service classifiers for content filtering. The most specific public account of the model is Microsoft's Azure engineering blog: the Dragon Copilot team built a fine-tuned model on a repository of clinical data that performed much better than the base foundational model with prompting alone, then runs a 'signals loop' — customer feedback telemetry continuously refines the model, and whenever a new foundational model ships they benchmark against it and update if there are significant gains. The fine-tuned model now outperforms base foundational models by roughly 50%. The base foundational model itself is never named. Dragon Copilot 6.0 began rolling out in the November 2026 deployment.
tools.conflict: Microsoft never names the base foundational model, only that it fine-tunes one and updates as new ones ship. Public statements range from 'fine-tuned generative AI' (2025 launch) to 'a variety of different models' in Copilot generally. Recorded as inferred for the architecture with the base explicitly marked undisclosed, rather than naming a GPT version nobody has confirmed.

tools.modelFamily: Microsoft Copilot multi-model routing (parent exposes GPT-6.x and Claude 5.x); Copilot Health's specific model not named
tools.notes: Copilot Health is a real, distinct product: Microsoft launched it on 2026-03-12 as 'a separate, secure space within Copilot' for Microsoft 365 Personal/Family/Premium subscribers in the US, connecting EHRs (HealthEx, 50,000+ US hospitals), labs (Function) and 50+ wearables, with a Health Profile and grounded answers sourced from credible health organizations selected using National Academy of Medicine principles, plus Harvard Health content. Microsoft never names the foundation model serving Copilot Health: its launch post only says it 'makes use of increasingly sophisticated AI' and points to the MAI-DxO medical diagnostic orchestrator research, and the support FAQ states only that data 'is not used to train AI models'. Microsoft Copilot as a product is explicitly a routed multi-model surface (GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5 as of late September 2026), and a clinician review of consumer AI health tools concluded Copilot Health runs on the 'same underlying models' as general-purpose assistants with a health-specific wrapper, but no source names the specific model behind the Health surface. Note: as of the support page's October 2026 update, Copilot Health is temporarily unavailable during the transition to the unified Copilot experience.
tools.conflict: Microsoft's broader Copilot stack is public (GPT-6 Sol / GPT-6.1 Sol from OpenAI, Claude Opus 5.5 / Sonnet 5.5 from Anthropic, with consumer 'Smart' mode on GPT-5), which invites the assumption that Copilot Health runs on one of these. No vendor source makes that link, so the model is recorded as undisclosed rather than inferred.

stack.v: EHR via HealthEx, labs via Function, 50+ wearables

tools.model: Apple Foundation Models (AFM) 3 family — on-device AFM 3 Core and AFM 3 Core Advanced; server-side AFM 3 Cloud / AFM 3 Cloud Pro in Private Cloud Compute (plus ADM 3 Cloud for images)
tools.modelFamily: Apple Foundation Models, 3rd generation (built in collaboration with Google)
tools.notes: Apple's Health app is explicitly 'built with Apple Intelligence at its core'; Apple has not published a per-feature mapping from AFM 3 models to individual Health features, so the model stack is disclosed at family level. The current generation (June 2026) is AFM 3: two on-device models (AFM 3 Core, a ~3B-parameter dense model, and AFM 3 Core Advanced, a 20B-parameter sparse model activating 1–4B parameters) and three server models on Private Cloud Compute (AFM 3 Cloud workhorse, AFM 3 Cloud Pro for agentic tool use and complex reasoning, and ADM 3 Cloud for images). AFM 3 Cloud Pro runs on NVIDIA GPUs in Google Cloud while keeping Apple's privacy guarantees. Separate from the AFM text models, Apple's at-home movement evaluations (flexibility, strength, balance, VO2 max) run entirely on device using vision-based AI models, and newer Watch sensing uses purpose-built ML models. Server-side AFM 3 Cloud usage is subject to daily limits, and Apple says paid expansion of server-model access is planned.
tools.conflict: No vendor page states which AFM 3 model (Core, Core Advanced, Cloud, or Cloud Pro) backs each Health app feature; the family-level mapping is an inference from Apple's statement that Health is 'built with Apple Intelligence at its core' plus AFM 3 being the current generation (2026-06-08). The 2025 generation (AFM On-Device 2025, AFM Server 2025) is now superseded.

tools.notes: Google says repeatedly and only that the coach is 'built with Gemini' / 'grounded in Gemini models' — it never names a Gemini version for the consumer Health product, so the family is disclosed but the specific model is not. Google's Gemini app release notes (2026-10-13) introduce 'Gemini 4 Argon' as the current frontier model, with Gemini 3.x Pro/Flash still in the lineup, but there is no statement tying a version to Health Coach. The Health Coach is a Gemini-powered multi-agent system in Google's research lineage (data-science, domain-expert and health-coach agents plus an orchestrator), grounded via Google Health research, the SHARP safety/quality evaluation framework, and a Consumer Health Advisory Panel. The research prototype Personal Health Agent was published in Nature (Oct 2026) and is described as built on Gemini 2.0 models. Google also ships open-weight health models separately (MedGemma 1.5, MedASR) and Health Connect, which is a pure on-device data store with no AI model. No user-facing model picker exists in Google Health.
tools.conflict: Google's public material names different Gemini versions for different health surfaces (Gemini 2.0 for the Personal Health Agent research prototype, 'latest Gemini models' for AI Mode, unspecified for Health Coach), and Google does not state which one serves the shipping Google Health app. Recorded as family-level 'Gemini' with version undisclosed rather than picking one.

tools.modelFamily: MedGemma (Gemma 3 backbone + SigLIP medical vision encoder); family also includes MedGemma 1 4B multimodal, 27B text-only, 27B multimodal
tools.notes: The latest MedGemma is MedGemma 1.5 4B, released 2026-01-13 as the only 1.5 variant (4B multimodal instruction-tuned, google/medgemma-1.5-4b-it). It is built on Gemma 3 (decoder-only transformer) with a SigLIP image encoder pre-trained on de-identified medical images, and adds CT/MRI volume interpretation, whole-slide histopathology, longitudinal chest X-ray comparison, bounding-box anatomical localization, lab-report extraction and text-EHR understanding over MedGemma 1 4B. Weights are open (Hugging Face + Vertex AI Model Garden) under the Health AI Developer Foundations licence, run on a single GPU via transformers/vLLM or a custom serving container, and are explicitly positioned as 'starting points for developers to evaluate and adapt' — so MedGemma is a developer foundation, not a shipped Google clinical product. Google's own health AI runs on Gemini (Personal Health LLM is 'a version of the Gemini model fine-tuned for health'; AMIE is a research system), while MedGemma/TxGemma are the open-weight developer line. Model choice is the developer's: pick 4B vs 27B, multimodal vs text-only, pre-trained vs instruction-tuned, then fine-tune; Google requires validation for any use case.
tools.conflict: Documentation lags the release: the HAI-DEF MedGemma landing page lists MedGemma 1.5 as 4B multimodal only, while the Hugging Face collection and GitHub README still describe only the MedGemma 1 lineup — the 27B variants were never refreshed to 1.5. There is no MedGemma 2, and the wider Gemma family has moved on (Gemma 4) without a medical refresh, so MedGemma remains a Gemma 3 derivative.

tools.modelFamily: Claude 5.5 (Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5) and Mythos-class Claude Fable 5.1 / Claude Mythos 5.1
tools.notes: Claude for Healthcare (announced 2026-01-11) is not a separately trained medical model — Anthropic says the feature set 'build[s] on top of major recent improvements we've made to Claude's general intelligence' and named Claude Opus 4.5 as the model backing it at launch; today's live lineup is Claude Opus 5.5 (2026-09-22), Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5, with Claude Fable 5.1 (2026-08-31) as a 'Covered Model' reachable by HIPAA-ready Enterprise and API customers, and Mythos/Opus/Sonnet under the Life Sciences Verification Program for biology-heavy work (2026-09-17). The clinical capability comes from connectors (CMS Coverage Database, ICD-10, NPI Registry, PubMed; HealthEx, Function, Apple Health, Android Health Connect for patients; Medidata, ClinicalTrials.gov, ToolUniverse, bioRxiv/medRxiv, Open Targets, ChEMBL, Owkin, Benchling, 10x Genomics, BioRender, Synapse, Wiley) plus Agent Skills (FHIR development, sample prior-authorization review, clinical-trial protocol drafting) and the anthropics/healthcare plugin with hosted MCP servers (clinical-note-extract, fhir, fraud-detection, icd10-cm, procedure-coding, prior-auth) — i.e. RAG/grounded retrieval over payer and literature databases with citations. Model choice is user-selectable through the Claude model picker and API model IDs; patient health data is explicitly not used for training, but Covered Models (Fable 5/5.1) require 30-day retention so zero-data-retention orgs cannot use them. The most recent healthcare-specific step is athenahealth's athenaPatient MCP (2026-11-02) letting patients query their own records through Claude.
tools.conflict: Anthropic's launch post (2026-01-11) states Claude Opus 4.5 powered the offering; Anthropic's current model docs say to start with Claude Opus 5.5 for most workloads, so the healthcare product almost certainly moved forward, but no Anthropic page pins the healthcare SKU to a specific model ID — 'Claude Opus 5.5' reflects the current default lineup, not a stated healthcare-specific model. Press at launch described 'models trained specifically for healthcare and life sciences tasks', but Anthropic's own wording is that it extends general-intelligence improvements, so any dedicated medical fine-tune is undisclosed.

tools.category: EHR vendor AI (Art, AI Charting, Emmie, Agent Factory)
tools.modelFamily: Multi-model via Microsoft Azure OpenAI + Epic's proprietary Cosmos foundation models
tools.notes: Epic does not name the LLM behind Art, AI Charting, Emmie, Penny or Agent Factory. Its own public AI page still describes a HIPAA-compliant pipeline that 'incorporates state-of-the-art language models, like GPT-4', and its product timeline records 'Epic supports GPT-4' in 2025. By February 2026 an Epic spokesperson said Epic 'continue[s] to work with Microsoft on AI Charting and use[s] a variety of different models through the Microsoft Azure platform', and Epic's VP of R&D Corey Miller said Epic 'generally uses different models for different specialties and tasks, and accesses those through Microsoft's Azure platform' — so Epic routes across frontier models rather than committing to one, and AI Charting is a separate product from Microsoft's DAX/Dragon. Health systems do get some model selection in Agent Factory: builders pick the model inside the agent portion of a flow, with per-million-token costs passed through. One concrete datapoint from a health-system build-a-thon (WVU Medicine, June 2026): the build environment ran on a single model, OpenAI's ChatGPT 5.1, with others expected to follow. Epic's own foundation model line is Cosmos Curiosity (formerly CoMET), a family of generative medical models trained on 300M+ de-identified Cosmos records that predict future medical events — a medical-event model, not a general-purpose LLM. Epic's AI Charting uses Microsoft Dragon for transcription (on Haiku/Canto devices) but generates notes with its own models.
tools.conflict: Epic's public AI marketing page still cites GPT-4, which is likely stale relative to a 2026 multi-model Azure stack (GPT-5.1 in the Agent Factory build environment as of June 2026; GPT-6.x available on Azure by late 2026). No Epic source names the model behind any specific shipped feature, so the current model per feature is recorded as undisclosed.
